title: The .NET Command-Line Interface
subtopics: Introducing single-file and file-based C# apps
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose of the .net command-line interface in a C#/.NET program.
Predict the result of the included C# example and verify the documented output.
Apply the .net command-line interface to a small task and identify one relevant boundary, limitation, or version requirement.

content.intro: The .NET Command-Line Interface is lesson 10 in Introduction to C#. The `dotnet` CLI creates, restores, builds, tests, runs, and publishes .NET projects. Run commands from the intended project directory and use `dotnet --info` to troubleshoot SDK selection.
content.why_it_matters: A language becomes useful when you can connect syntax to the tools that compile, run, and package an application. This lesson focuses on the .net command-line interface and shows how to verify the behavior instead of relying on assumptions.

content_blocks.title: A practical way to learn it
content_blocks.text: Start with the smallest valid case for the .net command-line interface. Predict the output, run or inspect the example in the stated toolchain, then change one input or rule and compare the result. For production code, record assumptions and verify boundary cases.

content_blocks.run_instructions: From a terminal, run `dotnet new console -n FirstCSharpApp`, change into the folder, put the snippet in Program.cs, and run `dotnet run`. CodeLeaf shows a reference output and does not execute C# in the browser.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Restore the documented snippet, rerun it locally in a compatible .NET project, and compare output. Remove temporary files or test data after checking them. Do not treat the in-page output panel as execution.

content_blocks.title: Version and reliability note
content_blocks.text: The `dotnet` CLI creates, restores, builds, tests, runs, and publishes .NET projects. Run commands from the intended project directory and use `dotnet --info` to troubleshoot SDK selection.

content.task: Try it yourself: create a small C# example that demonstrates the .net command-line interface. Change one input or implementation detail, predict the result, then check it locally and explain one edge case.
task_acceptance_criteria: The example demonstrates the .net command-line interface rather than only repeating its definition.
The result is checked locally or against a clearly documented reference output.
At least one relevant boundary, invalid-input case, or compatibility condition is considered.
hints: List the assumptions and expected behavior for the .net command-line interface before editing the code.
Change one variable or rule at a time; keep the previous output for comparison.
If behavior differs, confirm the compiler/target framework and consult the linked official documentation.
content.solution_notes: Suggested approach: identify the expected input and output, start from the smallest example, use the feature only where it clarifies the rule, and verify both a typical case and a boundary/failure case.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming the feature works identically on every target
common_mistakes.why: Language syntax, libraries, and runtime support are version-dependent.
common_mistakes.fix: Check the target framework and official versioned reference before using the feature.

common_mistakes.why: Boundary values, malformed input, and failure states often expose the real bug.
common_mistakes.fix: Add one typical input and one boundary or invalid case to the manual or automated checks.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating sample output as proof that the code ran
common_mistakes.why: The course reader uses static reference output for C# because it has no C# execution runner.
common_mistakes.fix: Run the snippet in a local .NET project or a separately isolated execution service.
